question: State your theme, then check that every element of your action line—the plot—exists to serve it.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: In a fully realized story, the action line—what we call “plot” in ﬁction—exists to serve the theme.

question: Write a theme statement and use it to focus both your reporting and your writing.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Theme gives the audience a sense of time well invested. (What’s the point of reading unless reading has a point?) But it also focuses the reporting and writing.

question: Reinforce your theme at every opportunity—in the lead, at each major turn, and especially at the last word before any page break or jump.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: As the story took shape, the text reﬂected theme at every opportunity. The lead emphasized Gary Wall’s barren, postaccident existence:

question: Locate your theme inside yourself—draw it from your own convictions about cause and effect in human lives, not from the external world.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A literary theme inevitably springs from the writer’s personal values, his or her highly individual understanding of cause and effect in human lives.

question: Don’t reject a theme because it is clichéd: the familiar principle becomes an eternal truth at the conceptual level.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: clichés may be an embarrassment at the sentence level, but they are at the heart of theme. “At the conceptual level,” Franklin wrote, “the cliché undergoes a strange metamorphosis: It becomes an eternal truth.”

question: Find the context that links your protagonist’s life with your readers’ own.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Connecting with readers means ﬁnding the context that links the lives of your protagonists with their own.

question: If your protagonist’s life seems alien to your audience, take special pains to demonstrate the connections to their own.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: If your protagonist lives a life that seems especially alien to your audience, you must take special pains to demonstrate connections.

question: Articulate the lesson your theme carries—the bigger the lesson, the more value it adds for your audience.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: When you think about it, every theme incorporates a lesson. That’s the value added that draws an audience to a story in the ﬁ rst place. The bigger the lesson, the more value added.

question: Find the extraordinary in the ordinary: tell the tale of an ordinary person facing the challenges of ordinary living.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: part of the job is to ﬁnd the extraordinary in the ordinary.

question: Don’t impose a theme on your story; find it in the material and extract it from the facts the world delivers.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: “It’s not something that you bring to the story. It’s something that you ﬁ nd in the story and extract from the story.”

question: When a theme won’t surface, search for an overall title for the story and its parts to orient your brain toward its essence, structure, and drive.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: “I’m always looking for an overall title,” he said, “as well as titles for the various parts and chapters. It’s a way of orienting your brain toward the essence of the story, also its structure and drive.”

question: Write a theme statement first and use it to find both the title and the shape of the story.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: First we come up with a theme statement, and we use that to ﬁ nd both the title and the shape of the story.

question: Express your theme as one clear, coherent sentence, not a single word.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: “A true theme is not a word but a sentence,” McKee says, “one clear, coherent sentence that expresses a story’s irreducible meaning.”

question: Write your theme statement around a transitive verb so the sentence answers “what?” and shows causality.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Because they answer the question “what?” sentences built around transitive verbs show causality. And causality is the essence of a theme that tells readers how the world works and how they can inﬂ uence it. Hence, “Action creates (what?) identity.”

question: State your theme in three parts—a character, the conflict (“leads to”), and the outcome—so it suggests the shape of your narrative.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: “Every good premise,” he said, “is composed of three parts, each of which is essential to a good play. Let us examine ‘Frugality leads to waste.’ The ﬁ rst part of this premise suggests character—a frugal character. The second part ‘leads to,’ suggests conﬂ ict, and the third part, ‘waste,’ suggests the end of the play.”

question: Use your theme statement as the standard for every decision—structure, reporting, title, and especially what to cut.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: So the theme statement suggests your structure. It guides your reporting. It helps you ﬁ nd a title. If you have to cut, it tells you what can go and what must stay.

question: Before writing anything, type “theme:” at the top of the file and puzzle out the noun-verb-noun structure of your statement.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Because a theme statement is so valuable, the ﬁ rst word I write on any project is always the same. I open a new computer screen and type “t- h- e- m- e.” Then I hit the colon key and sit there for a minute, puzzling over just the right noun- verb- noun structure for my statement.

question: Let the theme statement and outline guide your journey, then erase them when you arrive.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Then I’m off on the writer’s journey, secure in the knowledge that I know my destination. When I arrive, I erase the theme statement and outline.

question: Develop your theme statement with your editor early in the process so it becomes a shared standard for decisions about the story.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Hashing one out together provides common ground, a shared standard for making decisions about a story.
